1	\section{Where Single-Signal Selection Fails}\label{sec:selection_gap}
2	
3	\paragraph{Definitional vs.\ empirical.}
4	We decompose the correlation-selection gap into two layers.
5	The first is structural: four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates from a given input (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), so they estimate quality across inputs but cannot rank candidates within an instance---selection failure is a design property, not an empirical finding.
6	The second layer is empirical and constitutes the core diagnostic: LP---the only per-sample signal---suffers compression under constrained decoding, with 60\% of SciERC instances showing within-instance LP range below 0.041 nats (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}), effectively eliminating the variation needed for sample discrimination. This compression is model-intrinsic: free-form decoding yields nearly identical LP distributions (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}). Even where LP varies, selection gains depend on LP-quality alignment rather than degeneracy alone.
7	Cross-instance $\rho$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}) is attenuated by varying instance difficulty; within-instance $\rho$ directly measures whether LP discriminates candidates for a fixed input, making it the relevant predictor of selection success.
8

32	\begin{figure}[t]
33	\centering
34	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_selection_gap}
35	\caption{Correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Bars: QE $\rho$; line: $\Delta$F1 vs.\ greedy (3-seed mean). Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal outperforms greedy (all $p{\geq}0.29$). Dashed green: oracle headroom ($+11.4$\,pp; oracle headroom $=$ best-of-$N$ F1 $-$ greedy F1); dotted gray: random.}
36	\label{fig:selection_gap}
37	\end{figure}
38	
39	Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal outperforms greedy on SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}; Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}); the oracle shows 11.4\,pp headroom, but LP achieves $+0.2$\,pp ($p{=}0.29$), below MDE (${\approx}$1.5\,pp; $n{=}529$; Table~\ref{tab:power_analysis}).
40	The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
41	Few-NERD provides the definitive contrast: LP achieves $+1.39$\,pp ($p{<}0.001$; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.021$, selection family $k{=}21$)\footnote{Under global correction ($k{=}57$), LP-best selection reaches Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$ (BH $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.003$)---the only positive selection signal approaching significance under the conservative Holm procedure.} at low degeneracy (13.0\% vs.\ 12.2--67.9\%), while structural signals still degrade (VC $-1.79$, SJ $-2.14$\,pp; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
42	
43	\paragraph{Diagnostic framework.}
44	We identify two co-occurring factors that jointly characterize the gap:
45	(1)~instance degeneracy sets the ceiling (SciERC 12.2\%, CoNLL 61.7\%);
46	(2)~oracle headroom bounds the opportunity within non-degenerate instances (CoNLL ${\approx}4$\,pp vs.\ SciERC 11.4\,pp);
47	(3)~LP compression limits exploitation (Few-NERD within-instance $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$ vs.\ SciERC $\rho{\approx}0.26$).
48	Degeneracy does not predict LP gain across datasets ($\rho{=}0.052$, $n{=}23$, $p{=}0.81$; Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}), though it co-varies with LP within fixed settings ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
49	These conditions interact ($R^2{<}0$); on non-degenerate instances, $\alpha$ approaches zero ($0.000$--$0.161$) despite $\rho$ up to 0.45 (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
50	
51	\paragraph{Mechanistic evidence (Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic}).}
52	Why does signal alignment collapse? Probing experiments on Qwen2.5-7B\footnote{Probes use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (not the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B); Qwen3-8B's thinking mode may alter self-evaluation dynamics. Conclusions are architecture-specific.} reveal an \textit{introspection boundary}: hidden-state linear probes achieve entity-level AUROC $0.63$--$0.88$, substantially exceeding prompt-based self-judgment (ESJ AUROC $0.51$, indistinguishable from chance), yet cross-dataset transfer drops to $0.56$--$0.67$ (LODO).
53	Entity self-judgment, multi-round refinement ($-3.1$\,pp vs.\ greedy), and latent centroid selection ($-3.5$\,pp) all fail to improve over greedy decoding.
54	Entity quality is partially encoded in representations but inaccessible through the generation interface---consistent with the signal alignment collapse observed across all configurations.
55

36	\subsection{Trained Verifiers: High Discrimination, Low Transfer}\label{sec:verifier}
37

41	Even near-perfect entity classification cannot close the gap, indicating a structural bottleneck.

\section{Adaptive Methods}\label{sec:adaptive}

Since instance-level selection fails (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}), we present approaches that extract value from multi-sample generation beyond single-signal sample ranking.
Table~\ref{tab:method_summary} summarizes all 9 method categories evaluated; only cross-model ensembles yield a positive result, though on a single dataset.

{\footnotesize $^\dagger$Few-NERD only; SciERC $+0.2$\,pp ($p{=}0.29$). $^\ddagger$Seed-sensitive ($\sigma{=}0.48$\,pp).}
\end{table}

\subsection{Cross-Model Self-Consistency}\label{sec:cross_model}

Mixing samples from architecturally distinct models can partially bypass within-model degeneracy.
Combining 4 samples each from Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B (Few-NERD) yields $+0.42$\,pp over pure LLaMA ($p{<}0.001$, CI $[0.27, 0.58]$; $N{=}8$ total).
This observation is preliminary (single dataset, $n{=}4{+}4$ samples); cross-dataset validation is needed before drawing general conclusions.

\subsection{Trained Verifiers: High Discrimination, Low Transfer}\label{sec:verifier}

A LightGBM entity-level classifier (5 features: agreement count, LP, VC, SJ, FK) achieves AUC${=}0.923{\pm}0.002$ under out-of-fold evaluation, yet translates to only $+0.30$\,pp overall ($+1.28$ SciERC, $+0.02$ Few-NERD): frequency-based construction already captures most verifier signal.
Cross-dataset transfer is negative ($-0.76$ to $-1.02$\,pp on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:verifier_transfer}), confirming dataset-specific feature mappings.
Feature-level analysis reveals the source: LR coefficients for exact match (0.44 on SciERC vs.\ 1.47 on CoNLL) and voting confidence (0.06 vs.\ 0.49) shift drastically across datasets, as simpler entity types in CoNLL make agreement-based signals far more predictive than in SciERC's nested scientific entities.
Even near-perfect entity classification cannot close the gap, indicating a structural bottleneck.

1	\section{How Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}
2	
3	The diagnostic framework (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
4	Probe experiments use Qwen2.5-7B (not the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B used in main experiments); conclusions are architecture-specific.
5	We evaluate self-verification and diagnostic probes on Qwen2.5-7B\footnote{ESJ, MRSC, and LSC use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (zero-shot self-verification capability) rather than the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B used in the main experiments. Conclusion direction is consistent with the main experiments' negative results across all fine-tuned selection strategies. The pattern---selection failure across all signals---is independently confirmed in the Qwen3-8B main experiments, making the introspection boundary a model-independent finding within our tested scale. Probe conclusions are limited to the Qwen2.5 architecture; linear probes may underestimate representational capacity (nonlinear alternatives are left to future work).} fine-tuned for NER on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).
6	
7	\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
8	For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
9	Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
10	ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).
11	
12	\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
13	Following iterative self-refinement \cite{madaan2023selfrefine}, we re-prompt on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification; P(yes) separation between gold and non-gold entities is $0.0006$ ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
14	MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.
15	
16	\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
17	Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
18	Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.794$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) outperforms majority vote ($0.792$) but does not close the oracle gap ($0.882$).
19	
20	\paragraph{Hidden-state probe.}
21	A logistic regression on mean-pooled final-layer hidden states at entity spans achieves AUROC $0.636$ (Few-NERD), $0.882$ (CoNLL), $0.630$ (SciERC), evaluated with GroupKFold CV (5-fold ${\times}$ 3 seeds, groups${=}$source instance to prevent entity-level leakage; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).
22	All three exceed ESJ ($0.51$); only CoNLL approaches frequency agreement ($0.868$).
23	Cross-dataset transfer is weak: leave-one-dataset-out AUROC drops to $0.559$ (Few-NERD${\to}$CoNLL) and $0.671$ (CoNLL${\to}$Few-NERD), indicating that entity error patterns are dataset-specific rather than reflecting a universal introspection boundary, limiting probe-based approaches without per-dataset calibration.
24	At the sample level, an MLP probe closes only 13.9\% of the oracle gap on SciERC (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).
25	
26	\paragraph{The introspection boundary.}
27	Entity quality is partially encoded in hidden representations: a supervised probe (AUROC $0.63$\textendash$0.88$) consistently exceeds self-judgment (ESJ $0.51$) but only marginally exceeds multi-sample agreement ($0.87$) on CoNLL, suggesting consensus captures information beyond single-pass representations while the prompt interface fails to access even partial hidden-state signal.
28	LODO transfer drops to $0.56$\textendash$0.67$, so even direct hidden-state access would not yield a universal quality signal---consistent with the negative cross-dataset verifier transfer (\S\ref{sec:verifier}).
29

\section{How Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}

The diagnostic framework (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
Probe experiments use Qwen2.5-7B (not the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B used in main experiments); conclusions are architecture-specific.
We evaluate self-verification and diagnostic probes on Qwen2.5-7B\footnote{ESJ, MRSC, and LSC use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (zero-shot self-verification capability) rather than the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B used in the main experiments. Conclusion direction is consistent with the main experiments' negative results across all fine-tuned selection strategies. The pattern---selection failure across all signals---is independently confirmed in the Qwen3-8B main experiments, making the introspection boundary a model-independent finding within our tested scale. Probe conclusions are limited to the Qwen2.5 architecture; linear probes may underestimate representational capacity (nonlinear alternatives are left to future work).} fine-tuned for NER on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
Following iterative self-refinement \cite{madaan2023selfrefine}, we re-prompt on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification; P(yes) separation between gold and non-gold entities is $0.0006$ ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.794$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) outperforms majority vote ($0.792$) but does not close the oracle gap ($0.882$).

\paragraph{Hidden-state probe.}
A logistic regression on mean-pooled final-layer hidden states at entity spans achieves AUROC $0.636$ (Few-NERD), $0.882$ (CoNLL), $0.630$ (SciERC), evaluated with GroupKFold CV (5-fold ${\times}$ 3 seeds, groups${=}$source instance to prevent entity-level leakage; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).
All three exceed ESJ ($0.51$); only CoNLL approaches frequency agreement ($0.868$).
Cross-dataset transfer is weak: leave-one-dataset-out AUROC drops to $0.559$ (Few-NERD${\to}$CoNLL) and $0.671$ (CoNLL${\to}$Few-NERD), indicating that entity error patterns are dataset-specific rather than reflecting a universal introspection boundary, limiting probe-based approaches without per-dataset calibration.
At the sample level, an MLP probe closes only 13.9\% of the oracle gap on SciERC (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).

\paragraph{The introspection boundary.}
Entity quality is partially encoded in hidden representations: a supervised probe (AUROC $0.63$\textendash$0.88$) consistently exceeds self-judgment (ESJ $0.51$) but only marginally exceeds multi-sample agreement ($0.87$) on CoNLL, suggesting consensus captures information beyond single-pass representations while the prompt interface fails to access even partial hidden-state signal.
LODO transfer drops to $0.56$\textendash$0.67$, so even direct hidden-state access would not yield a universal quality signal---consistent with the negative cross-dataset verifier transfer (\S\ref{sec:verifier}).

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
2	
3	\paragraph{Test-time scaling and self-consistency.}\label{sec:yun_contrast}
4	Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} and best-of-$N$ with scaling laws \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys, gao2023scaling} yield large gains on reasoning; reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} and trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, li2023stepaware} target discrete-answer settings.
5	SC can fail when consistent outputs are wrong \cite{chen2023twofailures}; free-form \cite{chen2024usc} and atomic \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic} variants face limits where sub-output agreement does not yield selection gain.
6	\citet{yun2025price} identify diversity collapse under constrained decoding (Table~\ref{tab:differentiation}); our degeneracy adds quantitative diagnostics ($D$, $\alpha$, LP compression) absent from their account.
7	
8	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
9	\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE ($\rho$ up to 0.47); we extend to instance-level analysis: (1)~task-level $\rho$ masks instance-level degeneracy; (2)~we decompose failure into degeneracy and LP compression; (3)~pre-deployment diagnostics that task-level correlation cannot provide.
10	\citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose entity voting for zero-shot NER; \citet{xie2024selfimproving} report positive SC where zero-shot diversity is high.
11	
12	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR.}
13	Our selection instantiates MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling}; \citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our LP compression findings.
14	LP is well-calibrated at population level \cite{kadavath2022language, tian2023calibration} and motivated as a quality signal by noisy channel models \cite{yee2019noisy}, yet too compressed within instances for selection.
15	Complementary lines include semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic}, token-level uncertainty for misclassification detection \cite{vazhentsev2022uncertainty}, evidential NER uncertainty \cite{zhang2023ener}, uncertainty transmission for sequential labeling \cite{he2024uncertainty}, calibrated structured prediction \cite{kuleshov2022calibrated}, selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective}, and conformal prediction \cite{fisch2021conformal, angelopoulos2023conformal}.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Test-time scaling and self-consistency.}\label{sec:yun_contrast}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} and best-of-$N$ with scaling laws \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys, gao2023scaling} yield large gains on reasoning; reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} and trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, li2023stepaware} target discrete-answer settings.
SC can fail when consistent outputs are wrong \cite{chen2023twofailures}; free-form \cite{chen2024usc} and atomic \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic} variants face limits where sub-output agreement does not yield selection gain.
\citet{yun2025price} identify diversity collapse under constrained decoding (Table~\ref{tab:differentiation}); our degeneracy adds quantitative diagnostics ($D$, $\alpha$, LP compression) absent from their account.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE ($\rho$ up to 0.47); we extend to instance-level analysis: (1)~task-level $\rho$ masks instance-level degeneracy; (2)~we decompose failure into degeneracy and LP compression; (3)~pre-deployment diagnostics that task-level correlation cannot provide.
\citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose entity voting for zero-shot NER; \citet{xie2024selfimproving} report positive SC where zero-shot diversity is high.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR.}
Our selection instantiates MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling}; \citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our LP compression findings.
LP is well-calibrated at population level \cite{kadavath2022language, tian2023calibration} and motivated as a quality signal by noisy channel models \cite{yee2019noisy}, yet too compressed within instances for selection.
Complementary lines include semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic}, token-level uncertainty for misclassification detection \cite{vazhentsev2022uncertainty}, evidential NER uncertainty \cite{zhang2023ener}, uncertainty transmission for sequential labeling \cite{he2024uncertainty}, calibrated structured prediction \cite{kuleshov2022calibrated}, selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective}, and conformal prediction \cite{fisch2021conformal, angelopoulos2023conformal}.

\end{table}

\paragraph{Concurrent work.}
\citet{landesberg2026bon} independently document a correlation-selection gap in best-of-$N$ reasoning: global judge $r{=}0.47$ masks within-prompt $r{=}0.27$ (Table~\ref{tab:novelty_comparison}).
The independent concurrent discovery validates the generality of the correlation-selection gap as a cross-domain phenomenon; our contribution is the mechanistic diagnosis specific to structured prediction---entity-set degeneracy and LP compression have no analogue in Landesberg's single-score reasoning setting.

1	\section{Threshold Regime Analysis}\label{sec:theory_scaling}
2	
3	\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}
4	
5	Entity-level construction selects $\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha{+}1)\}$ under balanced set-overlap utility; $\alpha{=}1$ recovers majority vote (Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}).
6	Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$; weighting improves when $w_i$ correlates with instance quality but degrades otherwise (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
7	We select $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ at the elbow of the compression curve, where LP-best selection advantage transitions from $+1.5$\,pp (compressed) to $+4.6$\,pp (non-compressed; Appendix~\ref{app:fewnerd_epsilon}).
8	
9	\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}
10	
11	Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
12	The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
13	Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).
14	
15	\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
16	Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
17	Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
18	Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).
19	
20	\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}
21	
22	\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
23	For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
24	where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
25	For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).
26	
27	\noindent The decomposition is diagnostic rather than predictive: the three factors ($D$, $G_{\textup{nd}}$, $\alpha$) localize where aggregation fails rather than forecasting performance.
28	Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound but it captures only 3--12\% of actual gains (Figure~\ref{fig:bound}): $\alpha$---not $D$---is the bottleneck ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$), and the bound cannot be tightened by signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) or verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}).
29	Conclusions are stable across $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$; signal alignment ($\alpha{\approx}0.068$) is the binding constraint, $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter than the degeneracy threshold.
30	
31	\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
32	The decomposition is an illustrative directional analysis showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative diagnostic tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.578$--$0.644$ reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.
33	
34	MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
35	Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.
36

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
2	
3	\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling and best-of-$N$.}
4	Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} and best-of-$N$ with compute-optimal allocation \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} drive large gains on reasoning and code tasks.
5	Reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} and BoN scaling laws \cite{gao2023scaling} reduce or characterize inference cost, while trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify} learn per-sample scoring.
6	All target discrete-answer settings; structured prediction requires different aggregation because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.
7	
8	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
9	\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we diagnose degeneracy and LP compression as mechanisms that prevent this correlation from yielding selection gains.
10	\citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction; our approach aggregates stochastic samples from a single fine-tuned model without prompt engineering.
11	\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats) corroborates this for NER.
12	Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar}.
13	
14	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
15	Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling}; \citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs, while our diagnosis identifies degeneracy as the primary bottleneck.
16	Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} and confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence, xia2025survey} provide complementary model-internal alternatives; our QE signals with AUROC up to 0.82 connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective} and support abstention independent of sample selection.
17

\section{Notation}\label{app:notation}

\section{Robustness Analysis}\label{app:robustness}

\begin{figure}[t]

\label{fig:temperature_robustness}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.364 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.004.
FK NER $\rho$ drops by 0.022, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
LP exhibits the largest temperature effect on NER ($\rho{=}0.249$ at $T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $0.205$ at $T{=}1.0$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.044$), consistent with lower temperature concentrating probability mass and improving LP's discriminative power for quality estimation; RE $T{=}0.7$ LP data is not available.
Across all comparisons, the signal hierarchy is preserved at both temperatures on NER (SJ${>}$FK${>}$LP at $T{=}0.7$: $0.364{>}0.289{>}0.249$; at $T{=}1.0$: $0.360{>}0.267{>}0.205$).

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.411{\pm}0.010$ (three seeds: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410), a gain of $+0.047$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent (LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$), though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.042$ (range: $+0.039$ to $+0.044$) while LP gains only $+0.004$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is seed-dependent: Qwen SciERC gains range from $+0.005$ to $+0.023$ across seeds (mean $+0.016$), while LLaMA CoNLL yields $+0.039$ (3-seed mean); individual seed FK shifts vary substantially under the unified pipeline, so this should not be interpreted as a robust trend.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.030$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.034$).
SJ, EM, and VC scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows seed-dependent variation that does not constitute a reliable trend, structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.
At $N{=}16$, SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) while exhibiting lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$), a more stable alternative at higher sample sizes.

\paragraph{Transfer across model families.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct shows a similar SJ--FK ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.325{\pm}0.021$, FK $\rho{=}0.256{\pm}0.024$, $\Delta\rho{=}0.069$; permutation $p{=}0.06$, borderline).
On CoNLL, the gap across model families is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.

\paragraph{FK independence: instance-level permutation test.}\label{app:fk_independence}

To verify that Fleiss' $\kappa$ reflects genuine within-instance agreement rather than marginal-rate artifacts, we conduct instance-level permutation tests across three configurations.
For each instance, we permute sample labels 10{,}000 times to generate a null distribution of FK under independence, then compare the observed FK against this null via a one-sample $t$-test and permutation $p$-value.

\centering
\small
\caption{Instance-level FK independence test. Permutation tests confirm FK reflects true within-instance agreement (all $p{<}0.001$). Split-half reliability $r$ computed by randomly partitioning $N$ samples into two halves and correlating their FK scores.}

\toprule

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:fk_independence} reports the results.
All configurations reject the independence null at $p{<}0.001$ ($n{=}529$--$2{,}756$), FK captures genuine inter-sample agreement rather than chance label co-occurrence.
Split-half reliability ranges from $r{=}0.395$ (SciERC) to $r{=}0.578$ (CoNLL LLaMA), moderate stability: FK estimates from half the samples correlate positively with those from the other half, though the SciERC value suggests noisier estimation on harder tasks with fewer samples.
The higher FK means on CoNLL ($0.720$--$0.927$) vs.\ SciERC ($0.402$) mirror the difficulty gradient observed in the main quality estimation results.

NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE exhibits greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), translating consistency scores into calibrated confidence estimates is feasible for NER but remains challenging for compound extraction tasks.

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_signal_heatmap}
\caption{Quality estimation heatmap (Spearman $\rho$) across five signals and four configurations. Left: full evaluation set; right: conditional set (non-zero F1 instances). On the full set, structural signals dominate on SciERC NER while all signals converge on CoNLL. On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while LP RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.011$).}
\label{fig:signal_heatmap}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.

We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.

\begin{figure}[t]

Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.

- Non-degenerate subset construction footnote (line 107): **+7.08 pp** FewNERD (closest number, but different metric and still ≠ 8)

**Registry verification**: No experiment yields +8pp from any LP-based method on FewNERD. LP selection (exp_021_fewnerd_full, s42) = +1.36pp; 3-seed mean ≈ +1.38pp. Entity construction (exp_entity_construction, N=16 uniform) = +1.32pp.

**Likely cause**: Stale number from earlier framing revision (paper_framing.md also says "+8pp", suggesting the error originated there and propagated to tex).

**Fix**: Replace "+8 pp" with the correct number. If referring to LP selection: "+1.39 pp". If referring to LP-weighted entity construction: "+1.40 pp".

---

## ⚠️ WARNING

### W1. Selection table metric mismatch (micro vs macro F1)

**Location**: `single_signal.tex:12-30` (Table 2 / tab:selection)
**Issue**: Table is titled "Best-of-N selection (**macro** F1)" and shows Oracle=0.775, Greedy=0.645. Caption simultaneously states "baselines: 3-seed (Oracle=**0.781**, Greedy=**0.667**)" — these are **micro** F1 values.

| Metric | Oracle | Greedy | Headroom |
|--------|--------|--------|----------|
| Macro (table body) | 0.775 | 0.645 | 13.0 pp |
| Micro (caption text) | 0.781 | 0.667 | 11.4 pp |

The adjacent Figure 2 caption uses "oracle headroom (+11.4 pp)" — the micro-F1 headroom, not the macro-F1 headroom of the table it accompanies.

**Risk**: Reviewer notices headroom number doesn't match table arithmetic (0.775−0.645=13.0pp ≠ 11.4pp).

**Fix**: Either (a) remove micro baselines from caption, or (b) label explicitly: "macro-F1 baselines: Oracle=0.775, Greedy=0.645; micro-F1 reference: 0.781/0.667".

### W2. Limitations "consistent negative" across seeds

**Location**: `limitations.tex:1`
**Claim**: "Δ_SC = −0.74±0.57 pp, consistent negative"
**Registry data** (SciERC MV N=8, 3 seeds): s42=−0.74, s123=**+0.34**, s456=−0.84

One of three seeds is positive. If −0.74±0.57 is a confidence interval [−1.31, −0.17], "consistent negative" is defensible as the CI excludes zero. But −0.74 appears to be the single s42 value, not the 3-seed mean (which is −0.41). The ±0.57 doesn't match the 3-seed std (≈0.64) either.

**Fix**: Use 3-seed mean±std: "Δ_SC = −0.41±0.64 pp" or clarify what −0.74±0.57 represents.

### W3. Epoch confound LP delta reporting

**Location**: `experiments_main.tex:114`
**Claim**: "5-epoch training eliminates LP gains entirely (+1.39→+0.12±0.04 pp, 91% collapse)"
**Registry** (5-epoch FewNERD LP Δ, 3 seeds): s42=+0.07, s123=+0.09, s456=+0.12
- 3-seed mean = **0.093**, not 0.12
- 3-seed std = **0.025**, not 0.04
- Actual collapse = (1.39−0.093)/1.39 = **93.3%**, not 91%

The paper reports the maximum seed value (0.12) rather than the mean, and an inflated std (0.04 vs 0.025).

**Fix**: "+1.39→+0.09±0.03 pp, 93% collapse" (using 3-seed mean rounded).

### W4. WNUT-17 zero-F1 rate discrepancy

**Location**: `experiments_main.tex:10`
**Claim**: "WNUT-17 (1,287 social media instances, 51% zero F1)"
**Registry** (exp_003_ner_wnut17): **53.7%** zero F1

Discrepancy of 2.7pp. Could reflect different seeds, filtering, or a stale number.

**Fix**: Verify which number is correct and update.

### W5. RE zero-F1 rounding

**Location**: `introduction.tex:12`
**Claim**: "RE reveals a distinct bottleneck (40% zero-F1)"
**Registry** (exp_004_re_diagnostic): **43–47%** zero-F1 across configurations

Understated by 3–7pp. The paper_framing also says "43-47%", so the tex rounded down.

**Fix**: "~45% zero-F1" or "43–47% zero-F1".

### W6. FewNERD table SciERC greedy F1

**Location**: `experiments_main.tex:69` (tab:fewnerd, SciERC row)
**Claim**: Greedy = .667 (labeled "3-seed means")
**Registry**: s42=0.6617, s123=0.6633, s456=0.6631 → 3-seed mean = **0.6627**

0.6627 rounds to 0.663, not 0.667. Discrepancy of 0.004.

**Fix**: Change .667 to .663 (or verify if a different seed set / filtering yields .667).

### W7. Discussion std ratio lower bound

**Location**: `discussion.tex:6`
**Claim**: "LP std ratio 0.92–0.97×"
**Verification**: 0.97 confirmed (SciERC free-form ablation, exp_freeform_ablation). Source of 0.92 not found in registry. Could be from a different dataset/config, but unverified.

**Fix**: Verify 0.92 source and cite it, or narrow to "0.97×".

---

## ℹ️ INFO (no action needed)

### I1. Original Discussion/Limitations contradiction — RESOLVED

The task flagged: Discussion "+0.1pp over single-sample" vs Limitations "+0.4pp over greedy". These phrases **do not appear** in the current tex. The contradiction has been fixed in a prior revision.

### I2. Acceptable rounding throughout

| Claim | Source | Rounding |
|-------|--------|----------|
| "AUROC up to 0.82" | EM CoNLL Qwen = 0.816 | ✅ standard |
| "ρ up to 0.45" | EM CoNLL Qwen = 0.451 | ✅ conservative |
| "MV +0.6 pp at N=64" | Registry s42 = +0.64 | ✅ |
| "degeneracy 12–68%" | SciERC 12.2%, WNUT 67.9% | ✅ |
| "AUROC 0.63–0.88" probes | GroupKFold: 0.634–0.885 | ✅ |

### I3. Dataset instance counts: total vs evaluated

- FewNERD: 37,648 (setup) vs 32,565 (tab:fewnerd) — difference is gold-filtering (excluding empty-gold instances)
- CoNLL: 3,453 (setup) vs 2,756 (evaluation) — same reason
- SciERC: 551 (setup) vs 529 (evaluation) — same reason
All consistent with stated filtering methodology.

### I4. Abstract "<1 pp" ambiguity

"instance-level selection yields <1 pp" — FewNERD LP gives +1.39pp, but LP is a **per-sample** signal, not instance-level. The paper carefully defines "instance-level" signals as those producing one score per input (4 of 5 signals). Under this definition, the claim is correct. However, a casual reader might interpret "instance-level selection" as "selection at the instance level" and see a contradiction.

### I5. MV delta 3-seed means vs single-seed registry

Most MV and LP deltas in the paper use 3-seed means while the primary registry entries are seed 42. All verified 3-seed means are approximately consistent with individual seed values (within expected seed variance).

1	# Claim Audit Report — struct_self_consist_ie
2	
3	**Date**: 2026-05-19  
4	**Scope**: All quantitative claims in `docs/paper/sections/` cross-verified against experiment registry and paper_framing.md  
5	**Method**: Extracted every numerical claim (ρ, AUROC, F1, pp-delta, percentages), traced to source experiment, compared.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## ❌ Inconsistencies Requiring Fix
10	
11	### 1. WNUT VC ρ inconsistency within paper (0.724 vs 0.730)
12	
13	| Location | Value |
14	|----------|-------|
15	| experiments.tex:48 | VC ρ=0.724 |
16	| experiments.tex:104 | VC ρ=0.730 |
17	| appendix.tex:217 (tab:wnut) | VC .724 |
18	| appendix.tex:226 | VC ρ=0.724 |
19	
20	**Verdict**: 0.724 is the tabulated value, used 3× consistently. The 0.730 on line 104 is a **typo**.  
21	**Fix**: Change experiments.tex:104 from `VC $\rho{=}0.730$` to `VC $\rho{=}0.724$`.
22	
23	### 2. SciERC AUROC in Table 1 vs registry (systematic offset)
24	
25	Paper Table 1 SciERC AUROC vs registry `exp_012_rerun_1024` (same ρ values, so same data):
26	
27	| Signal | Paper AUC | Registry AUROC | Δ |
28	|--------|-----------|---------------|-----|
29	| VC | .663 | .684 | -2.1pp |
30	| SJ | .650 | .692 | -4.2pp |
31	| FK | .602 | .629 | -2.7pp |
32	| EM | .614 | .749 | **-13.5pp** |
33	| LP | .578 | .578 | 0pp |
34	
35	ρ values match to 3 decimal places (confirming same source data), but AUROC diverges except for LP. The EM gap (0.614 vs 0.749) is extreme. CoNLL AUROC values match the registry within 1pp.
36	
37	**Hypothesis**: Different AUROC binarization threshold or pipeline for SciERC. The SciERC median F1 may have tied instances handled differently.  
38	**Action required**: Verify which AUROC pipeline produced Table 1. If the registry values are correct, Table 1 SciERC AUROC column needs updating. This also affects:
39	- Abstract/Introduction "AUROC up to 0.82" → still valid (CoNLL EM 0.816 matches registry)
40	- But SciERC EM AUROC should be ~0.749, not 0.614
41	
42	### 3. CoNLL LP selection Δ: Table 3 vs Appendix cross-selection table
43	
44	| Source | Greedy | LP F1 | LP Δ |
45	|--------|--------|-------|------|
46	| Table 3 (experiments.tex:122) | .908 | — | **-0.85pp** |
47	| Appendix tab:cross_selection (appendix.tex:248) | .908 | .897 | **-1.1pp** |
48	
49	Both claim 3-seed means, Qwen/CoNLL N=8. The Δ values (-0.85pp vs -1.1pp) are inconsistent.  
50	**Fix**: Reconcile these two tables. Check whether different seed combinations or averaging methods were used.
51	
52	### 4. WNUT-17 zero-F1 rate inconsistency within paper
53	
54	| Location | Value |
55	|----------|-------|
56	| experiments.tex:12 (dataset description) | "52% zero F1" |
57	| experiments.tex:103 | "51% of instances yield F1=0" |
58	| limitations.tex:3 | "51% F1=0" |
59	
60	**Fix**: Unify to one value. If it's N=8 data, verify the exact percentage and use consistently.
61	
62	---
63	
64	## ⚠️ Ambiguous/Unverifiable Claims
65	
66	### 5. "13–87% degeneracy" in Introduction (line 15)
67	
68	The introduction says "instance degeneracy (13–87% across our benchmarks)."
69	
70	- 13% ≈ FewNERD (10.1–13.1% depending on seed) ✓
71	- 87% = LLaMA CoNLL N=16 (registry: 86.5–86.7%) — this is a specific **model×dataset×N** configuration, not a benchmark
72	
73	The appendix (line 232) confirms: "On CoNLL, 48–87% of instances produce identical outputs" — spanning Qwen N=8 (48%) to LLaMA N=16 (87%).
74	
75	**Issue**: "across our benchmarks" suggests cross-dataset variation, but 87% comes from a specific model+N configuration within CoNLL. The dataset-only range is ~10–68% (FewNERD to WNUT).  
76	**Recommendation**: Change to "across our experimental configurations" or specify: "(13% on Few-NERD to 87% on CoNLL under LLaMA at N=16)".
77	
78	### 6. CoNLL degeneracy 48.4% labeled as N=8 in Table 3
79	
80	Table 3 caption: "Qwen3-8B, N=8, T=1.0". CoNLL Degen.% = 48.4%.
81	
82	But `tab:degeneracy` (appendix.tex:362) shows: "CoNLL 8B (N=16)" = 48.4%.
83	
84	Registry `exp_002_conll_n16` (N=16, seed 42): degen_rate = 0.4844 (48.4%).
85	
86	No N=8 CoNLL degeneracy rate found in registry. With fewer samples (N=8), ALL having identical F1 is easier, so N=8 degeneracy should be **higher** than N=16's 48.4%.
87	
88	**Risk**: Table 3 may be using the N=16 degeneracy value in an N=8 context.  
89	**Action**: Verify the N=8 CoNLL degeneracy from the actual N=8 experiment data.
90	
91	### 7. FewNERD degeneracy 13.8% vs registry data
92	
93	Paper Table 3: FewNERD degen = 13.8%.
94	
95	Registry individual seeds (all N=8):
96	- Seed 42 (exp_021_fewnerd_full): 10.1%
97	- Seed 123: 13.1%
98	- Seed 456: 12.1%
99	- Seed 789: 11.8%
100	
101	3-seed mean (42/123/456): (10.1 + 13.1 + 12.1) / 3 = **11.8%** ≠ 13.8%  
102	4-seed mean: (10.1 + 13.1 + 12.1 + 11.8) / 4 = **11.8%** ≠ 13.8%
103	
104	**Source of 13.8% unclear.** No seed combination produces this value. Could be from a different computation or epoch checkpoint.
105	
106	### 8. FewNERD LP global ρ = .220 in Table 3 vs seed 42 = 0.422
107	
108	Table 3 says LP ρ = .220 (3-seed mean). Registry seed 42: lp_global_rho = 0.4215. Seed 789: lp_rho_global = 0.1788.
109	
110	This implies seeds 123/456 have very low LP ρ (~0.12 each) for the 3-seed mean to be 0.22. The seed variance (0.18–0.42) is extremely high for Spearman ρ, which is unusual.
111	
112	**Cannot verify** from available registry data (seeds 123/456 lack LP ρ).  
113	**Recommendation**: Verify the 3-seed LP ρ values and consider reporting seed-specific values to acknowledge this variance.
114	
115	### 9. WNUT LP ρ: paper -0.446 vs registry -0.410
116	
117	Paper Table 3: LP ρ = -.446 (claimed N=8).  
118	Registry exp_003_ner_wnut17 (N=16): rho_logprob_full = -0.414.  
119	Registry exp_003_wnut17_eval (N=16): rho_logprob_full = -0.409.
120	
121	Different N values (paper N=8, registry N=16), so some difference is expected. But no N=8 WNUT data found in registry to verify.
122	
123	### 10. Entity construction Δ: paper vs registry (protocol mismatch)
124	
125	Paper (multi-seed mean) vs registry (5-fold CV):
126	
127	| Dataset | Paper LP Δ | Registry LP Δ | Paper Unif Δ | Registry Unif Δ |
128	|---------|-----------|--------------|-------------|----------------|
129	| SciERC | +1.02pp | +1.67pp | +0.74pp | +1.12pp |
130	| FewNERD | +1.40pp | +0.88pp | +0.74pp | +0.32pp |
131	| CoNLL | -0.39pp | -0.39pp | — | — |
132	
133	Large differences on SciERC and FewNERD. The paper uses "multi-seed mean±σ" (averaging results from different training seeds), while the registry uses "5-fold CV, bootstrap B=10000" (within one model). These are legitimately different evaluation protocols, so direct comparison is invalid.
134	
135	**However**: The direction of difference is inconsistent — registry is higher than paper on SciERC but lower on FewNERD. This means multi-seed averaging isn't simply scaling all values down.  
136	**Recommendation**: Source the individual seed construction results to verify the multi-seed means match.
137	
138	---
139	
140	## ⚠️ Known Contradiction (from task description)
141	
142	**"Discussion '+0.1pp over single-sample' vs Limitations '+0.4pp over greedy'"**
143	
144	**Status**: Not found in current paper text.
145	
146	The closest matches are:
147	- Experiments §5.5 (scaling): "LP selection fails (SciERC −0.1pp, CoNLL −0.4pp)" — these are 72B zero-shot LP selection results, different datasets, both negative. Not contradictory.
148	- TOST appendix table: SJ NER Δ = +0.1pp (vs single-sample) — this is in the appendix, not Discussion.
149	- Limitations: "LP×VC combinations yield at most +0.2pp over greedy" — 0.2pp, not 0.4pp.
150	
151	**Conclusion**: The contradiction may have been resolved in the current paper version, or the task description references numbers from an earlier draft. The current paper does not contain this specific conflict.
152	
153	---
154	
155	## ✅ Verified Claims
156	
157	### Abstract & Introduction
158	| Claim | Source | Registry/Verified Value | Status |
159	|-------|--------|------------------------|--------|
160	| ρ up to 0.45 | CoNLL EM | exp_002: EM rho=0.4507 → 0.45 | ✅ |
161	| AUROC up to 0.82 | CoNLL EM | exp_002: EM AUROC=0.8156 → 0.82 | ✅ |
162	| +5–8pp F1 at 80% coverage | Selective pred. | exp_selective_prediction: SciERC +5.0, CoNLL +8.4, FewNERD +6.2 | ✅ |

# Claim Audit Report — struct_self_consist_ie

**Date**: 2026-05-19  
**Scope**: All quantitative claims in `docs/paper/sections/` cross-verified against experiment registry and paper_framing.md  
**Method**: Extracted every numerical claim (ρ, AUROC, F1, pp-delta, percentages), traced to source experiment, compared.

---

## ❌ Inconsistencies Requiring Fix

### 1. WNUT VC ρ inconsistency within paper (0.724 vs 0.730)

| Location | Value |
|----------|-------|
| experiments.tex:48 | VC ρ=0.724 |
| experiments.tex:104 | VC ρ=0.730 |
| appendix.tex:217 (tab:wnut) | VC .724 |
| appendix.tex:226 | VC ρ=0.724 |

**Verdict**: 0.724 is the tabulated value, used 3× consistently. The 0.730 on line 104 is a **typo**.  
**Fix**: Change experiments.tex:104 from `VC $\rho{=}0.730$` to `VC $\rho{=}0.724$`.

### 2. SciERC AUROC in Table 1 vs registry (systematic offset)

Paper Table 1 SciERC AUROC vs registry `exp_012_rerun_1024` (same ρ values, so same data):

| Signal | Paper AUC | Registry AUROC | Δ |
|--------|-----------|---------------|-----|
| VC | .663 | .684 | -2.1pp |
| SJ | .650 | .692 | -4.2pp |
| FK | .602 | .629 | -2.7pp |
| EM | .614 | .749 | **-13.5pp** |
| LP | .578 | .578 | 0pp |

ρ values match to 3 decimal places (confirming same source data), but AUROC diverges except for LP. The EM gap (0.614 vs 0.749) is extreme. CoNLL AUROC values match the registry within 1pp.

**Hypothesis**: Different AUROC binarization threshold or pipeline for SciERC. The SciERC median F1 may have tied instances handled differently.  
**Action required**: Verify which AUROC pipeline produced Table 1. If the registry values are correct, Table 1 SciERC AUROC column needs updating. This also affects:
- Abstract/Introduction "AUROC up to 0.82" → still valid (CoNLL EM 0.816 matches registry)
- But SciERC EM AUROC should be ~0.749, not 0.614

### 3. CoNLL LP selection Δ: Table 3 vs Appendix cross-selection table

| Source | Greedy | LP F1 | LP Δ |
|--------|--------|-------|------|
| Table 3 (experiments.tex:122) | .908 | — | **-0.85pp** |
| Appendix tab:cross_selection (appendix.tex:248) | .908 | .897 | **-1.1pp** |

Both claim 3-seed means, Qwen/CoNLL N=8. The Δ values (-0.85pp vs -1.1pp) are inconsistent.  
**Fix**: Reconcile these two tables. Check whether different seed combinations or averaging methods were used.

### 4. WNUT-17 zero-F1 rate inconsistency within paper

| Location | Value |
|----------|-------|
| experiments.tex:12 (dataset description) | "52% zero F1" |
| experiments.tex:103 | "51% of instances yield F1=0" |
| limitations.tex:3 | "51% F1=0" |

**Fix**: Unify to one value. If it's N=8 data, verify the exact percentage and use consistently.

---

## ⚠️ Ambiguous/Unverifiable Claims

### 5. "13–87% degeneracy" in Introduction (line 15)

The introduction says "instance degeneracy (13–87% across our benchmarks)."

- 13% ≈ FewNERD (10.1–13.1% depending on seed) ✓
- 87% = LLaMA CoNLL N=16 (registry: 86.5–86.7%) — this is a specific **model×dataset×N** configuration, not a benchmark

The appendix (line 232) confirms: "On CoNLL, 48–87% of instances produce identical outputs" — spanning Qwen N=8 (48%) to LLaMA N=16 (87%).

**Issue**: "across our benchmarks" suggests cross-dataset variation, but 87% comes from a specific model+N configuration within CoNLL. The dataset-only range is ~10–68% (FewNERD to WNUT).  
**Recommendation**: Change to "across our experimental configurations" or specify: "(13% on Few-NERD to 87% on CoNLL under LLaMA at N=16)".

### 6. CoNLL degeneracy 48.4% labeled as N=8 in Table 3

Table 3 caption: "Qwen3-8B, N=8, T=1.0". CoNLL Degen.% = 48.4%.

But `tab:degeneracy` (appendix.tex:362) shows: "CoNLL 8B (N=16)" = 48.4%.

Registry `exp_002_conll_n16` (N=16, seed 42): degen_rate = 0.4844 (48.4%).

No N=8 CoNLL degeneracy rate found in registry. With fewer samples (N=8), ALL having identical F1 is easier, so N=8 degeneracy should be **higher** than N=16's 48.4%.

**Risk**: Table 3 may be using the N=16 degeneracy value in an N=8 context.  
**Action**: Verify the N=8 CoNLL degeneracy from the actual N=8 experiment data.

### 7. FewNERD degeneracy 13.8% vs registry data

Paper Table 3: FewNERD degen = 13.8%.

Registry individual seeds (all N=8):
- Seed 42 (exp_021_fewnerd_full): 10.1%
- Seed 123: 13.1%
- Seed 456: 12.1%
- Seed 789: 11.8%

3-seed mean (42/123/456): (10.1 + 13.1 + 12.1) / 3 = **11.8%** ≠ 13.8%  
4-seed mean: (10.1 + 13.1 + 12.1 + 11.8) / 4 = **11.8%** ≠ 13.8%

**Source of 13.8% unclear.** No seed combination produces this value. Could be from a different computation or epoch checkpoint.

### 8. FewNERD LP global ρ = .220 in Table 3 vs seed 42 = 0.422

Table 3 says LP ρ = .220 (3-seed mean). Registry seed 42: lp_global_rho = 0.4215. Seed 789: lp_rho_global = 0.1788.

This implies seeds 123/456 have very low LP ρ (~0.12 each) for the 3-seed mean to be 0.22. The seed variance (0.18–0.42) is extremely high for Spearman ρ, which is unusual.

**Cannot verify** from available registry data (seeds 123/456 lack LP ρ).  
**Recommendation**: Verify the 3-seed LP ρ values and consider reporting seed-specific values to acknowledge this variance.

### 9. WNUT LP ρ: paper -0.446 vs registry -0.410

Paper Table 3: LP ρ = -.446 (claimed N=8).  
Registry exp_003_ner_wnut17 (N=16): rho_logprob_full = -0.414.  
Registry exp_003_wnut17_eval (N=16): rho_logprob_full = -0.409.

Different N values (paper N=8, registry N=16), so some difference is expected. But no N=8 WNUT data found in registry to verify.

### 10. Entity construction Δ: paper vs registry (protocol mismatch)

Paper (multi-seed mean) vs registry (5-fold CV):

| Dataset | Paper LP Δ | Registry LP Δ | Paper Unif Δ | Registry Unif Δ |
|---------|-----------|--------------|-------------|----------------|
| SciERC | +1.02pp | +1.67pp | +0.74pp | +1.12pp |
| FewNERD | +1.40pp | +0.88pp | +0.74pp | +0.32pp |
| CoNLL | -0.39pp | -0.39pp | — | — |

Large differences on SciERC and FewNERD. The paper uses "multi-seed mean±σ" (averaging results from different training seeds), while the registry uses "5-fold CV, bootstrap B=10000" (within one model). These are legitimately different evaluation protocols, so direct comparison is invalid.

**However**: The direction of difference is inconsistent — registry is higher than paper on SciERC but lower on FewNERD. This means multi-seed averaging isn't simply scaling all values down.  
**Recommendation**: Source the individual seed construction results to verify the multi-seed means match.

---

**"Discussion '+0.1pp over single-sample' vs Limitations '+0.4pp over greedy'"**

**Status**: Not found in current paper text.

The closest matches are:
- Experiments §5.5 (scaling): "LP selection fails (SciERC −0.1pp, CoNLL −0.4pp)" — these are 72B zero-shot LP selection results, different datasets, both negative. Not contradictory.
- TOST appendix table: SJ NER Δ = +0.1pp (vs single-sample) — this is in the appendix, not Discussion.
- Limitations: "LP×VC combinations yield at most +0.2pp over greedy" — 0.2pp, not 0.4pp.

**Conclusion**: The contradiction may have been resolved in the current paper version, or the task description references numbers from an earlier draft. The current paper does not contain this specific conflict.

# Claim Audit Report — struct_self_consist_ie (v2)

**Date**: 2026-05-22 (supersedes v1 from 2026-05-19)
**Scope**: All quantitative claims in `docs/paper/sections/*.tex` cross-verified against experiment registry and paper_framing.md
**Method**: Extracted every numerical claim (ρ, AUROC, F1, pp-delta, percentages), traced to source experiment, compared.

---

## Executive Summary

- **1 Critical**: unsupported "+8 pp" claim in experiments section (internal contradiction)
- **7 Warnings**: metric mixing, imprecise multi-seed reporting, rounding inconsistencies
- **5 Info**: acceptable rounding, resolved prior contradictions, ambiguous but defensible wording
- The originally flagged Discussion/Limitations contradiction ("+0.1pp" vs "+0.4pp") **no longer exists** in current tex
- Several issues from v1 audit (SciERC AUROC, WNUT VC ρ typo) appear to have been fixed

---

## ❌ CRITICAL

### C1. Unsupported "+8 pp" LP-best claim on FewNERD

**Location**: `experiments_main.tex:89`
**Claim**: "the optimal strategy is dataset-dependent (LP-best +8 pp on Few-NERD vs. MV +0.61 pp on CoNLL)"
**Internal contradiction** — three places in the same paper give different numbers:
- Same file, `tab:fewnerd` (line 70): LP Δ = **+1.39 pp** on FewNERD
- Same file, prescriptive §5 (line 107): LP-weighted construction = **+1.40 pp** on FewNERD
- `adaptive.tex` method summary table (line 17): LP selection = **+1.39 pp (FN)**
- Prescriptive footnote (line 107): non-degenerate subset construction = **+7.08 pp** (closest number, but different metric and still ≠ 8)

**Registry verification**: No experiment yields +8pp from any LP-based method on FewNERD.
- LP selection (exp_021_fewnerd_full, s42) = +1.36pp; 3-seed mean ≈ +1.38pp
- Entity construction (exp_entity_construction, N=16 uniform) = +1.32pp

**Likely cause**: Stale number from earlier framing revision (paper_framing.md also says "+8pp" in the strategy table, suggesting the error originated there and propagated to tex).

**Fix**: Replace "+8 pp" with "+1.39 pp" (LP selection) or "+1.40 pp" (LP-weighted construction) in `experiments_main.tex:89`.

---

## ⚠️ WARNING

### W1. Selection table metric mismatch (micro vs macro F1)

**Location**: `single_signal.tex:12-30` (Table 2 / tab:selection)
**Issue**: Table is titled "Best-of-N selection (**macro** F1)" and body shows Oracle=0.775, Greedy=0.645. Caption simultaneously states "baselines: 3-seed (Oracle=**0.781**, Greedy=**0.667**)" — these match **micro** F1 values from the registry.

| Metric | Oracle | Greedy | Headroom |
|--------|--------|--------|----------|
| Macro (table body) | 0.775 | 0.645 | 13.0 pp |
| Micro (caption text) | 0.781 | 0.667 | 11.4 pp |

The adjacent Figure 2 caption uses "oracle headroom (+11.4 pp)" — the micro-F1 headroom, not the macro-F1 headroom from the table it accompanies.

**Risk**: Reviewer notices headroom 0.775−0.645=13.0pp ≠ 11.4pp stated in the figure.
**Fix**: Either (a) remove micro baselines from caption, or (b) label explicitly: "macro-F1 baselines in table; micro-F1 reference: Oracle=0.781, Greedy=0.667".

### W2. Limitations "consistent negative" across seeds

**Location**: `limitations.tex:1`
**Claim**: "Δ_SC = −0.74±0.57 pp, consistent negative"
**Registry** (SciERC MV N=8, 3 seeds): s42=−0.74, s123=**+0.34**, s456=−0.84

Issues:
1. −0.74 is the s42 value, not the 3-seed mean (which is −0.41)
2. ±0.57 doesn't match 3-seed std (≈0.64)
3. "Consistent negative" is contradicted by s123=+0.34 (positive)

**Fix**: Use 3-seed mean±std: "Δ_SC = −0.41±0.64 pp" and soften "consistent negative" to "negative on average".

### W3. Epoch confound LP delta reporting

**Location**: `experiments_main.tex:114`
**Claim**: "5-epoch training eliminates LP gains entirely (+1.39→+0.12±0.04 pp, 91% collapse)"
**Registry** (5-epoch FewNERD LP Δ, 3 seeds): s42=+0.07, s123=+0.09, s456=+0.12
- 3-seed mean = **0.093**, not 0.12
- 3-seed std ≈ **0.025**, not 0.04
- Actual collapse = (1.39−0.093)/1.39 = **93.3%**, not 91%

The paper reports the maximum seed value (0.12) rather than the mean (0.093), with an inflated std.
**Fix**: "+1.39→+0.09±0.03 pp, 93% collapse"

### W4. WNUT-17 zero-F1 rate discrepancy

**Location**: `experiments_main.tex:10`
**Claim**: "WNUT-17 (1,287 social media instances, 51% zero F1)"
**Registry** (exp_003_ner_wnut17): **53.7%** zero F1
**v1 audit** also flagged internal inconsistency (51% vs 52% within paper).

**Fix**: Verify the correct value and unify across all mentions.

### W5. RE zero-F1 rounding

**Location**: `introduction.tex:12`
**Claim**: "RE reveals a distinct bottleneck (40% zero-F1)"
**Registry** (exp_004_re_diagnostic): **43–47%** zero-F1 across configurations
**paper_framing.md** also says "43-47%"

Understated by 3–7pp.
**Fix**: "~45% zero-F1" or "43–47% zero-F1".

### W6. FewNERD table SciERC greedy F1

**Location**: `experiments_main.tex:69` (tab:fewnerd, SciERC row)
**Claim**: Greedy = .667 (labeled "3-seed means")
**Registry**: s42=0.6617, s123=0.6633, s456=0.6631 → 3-seed mean = **0.6627**

0.6627 rounds to 0.663, not 0.667. Discrepancy of 0.004.
**Fix**: Change .667 to .663 (or verify if a different seed set or filtering yields .667).

### W7. Discussion std ratio lower bound

**Location**: `discussion.tex:6`
**Claim**: "LP std ratio 0.92–0.97×"
**Verification**: 0.97 confirmed (SciERC free-form ablation, exp_freeform_ablation). Source of 0.92 not found in registry.

**Fix**: Verify 0.92 source and cite it, or narrow to "≈0.97×".

---

## ℹ️ INFO (no action needed)

### I1. Original Discussion/Limitations contradiction — RESOLVED

The task flagged: Discussion "+0.1pp over single-sample" vs Limitations "+0.4pp over greedy". These phrases **do not appear** in the current tex. The contradiction has been fixed in a prior revision.

### I2. Acceptable rounding throughout

| Claim | Source | Rounding |
|-------|--------|----------|
| "AUROC up to 0.82" | EM CoNLL Qwen = 0.816 | ✅ standard |
| "ρ up to 0.45" | EM CoNLL Qwen = 0.451 | ✅ conservative |
| "MV +0.6 pp at N=64" | Registry s42 = +0.64 | ✅ |
| "degeneracy 12–68%" | SciERC 12.2%, WNUT 67.9% | ✅ |
| "AUROC 0.63–0.88" probes | GroupKFold: 0.634–0.885 | ✅ |
| "probe 0.88 vs self-judgment 0.51" | CoNLL probe 0.885, ESJ 0.512 | ✅ |

### I3. Dataset instance counts: total vs evaluated (consistent)

- FewNERD: 37,648 (setup) vs 32,565 (tab:fewnerd) — gold-filtering
- CoNLL: 3,453 (setup) vs 2,756 (evaluation) — gold-filtering
- SciERC: 551 (setup) vs 529 (evaluation) — gold-filtering
All consistent with stated filtering methodology.

### I4. Abstract "<1 pp" ambiguity

"instance-level selection yields <1 pp" — FewNERD LP gives +1.39pp, but LP is a **per-sample** signal, not instance-level. The paper carefully defines "instance-level" signals as those producing one score per input (4 of 5 signals). Under this definition, the claim is correct. A casual reader might misinterpret "instance-level selection" as "selection at the instance level."

### I5. v1 audit issues — status

Several issues from the 2026-05-19 v1 audit appear resolved in current tex:
- SciERC AUROC values in Table 1 now match registry (previously had systematic offset)
- The 0.82 AUROC claim remains valid (CoNLL EM 0.816)

Issues potentially still present from v1 (could not fully verify due to appendix size):
- CoNLL LP Δ mismatch between Table 3 and Appendix cross-selection table (−0.85 vs −1.1pp)
- FewNERD degeneracy 13.0% in tab:fewnerd vs registry individual seeds (10.1–13.1%); 3-seed mean ≈ 11.8%. Paper shows 13.0% which could be seed 123 alone.

---

## Cross-Chapter Consistency Matrix

| Claim | Abstract | Intro | Experiments | Discussion | Limitations | Conclusion |
|-------|----------|-------|-------------|------------|-------------|------------|
| AUROC ≤0.82 | 0.82 ✅ | 0.82 ✅ | Tab: 0.816 ✅ | — | — | — |
